category.name: Data exfiltration & DLP
category.description: Data leaving the organization: DLP alerts, cloud and USB exfiltration, leaked or exposed datasets, and accidental disclosure.

playbooks.name: DLP alert: PII emailed to an external address
playbooks.summary: Use when a DLP policy fires on an outbound email carrying personal data (SSNs, national IDs, customer records) to a recipient outside the organization.

preparation: Confirm DLP policies for SSN, national ID and customer-record patterns are enforced on the mail gateway, not audit-only
Keep DLP incident retention long enough to retrieve the matched attachment and message headers
Agree with Legal and Privacy who decides whether a DLP hit becomes a reportable breach
Maintain a list of sanctioned external partners and domains allowed to receive PII
identification: Pull the DLP incident: matched rule, match count, sender, recipients, subject and attachment names
Open the quarantined or delivered attachment in a sandboxed viewer and count the data subjects exposed
Check whether the recipient domain is a contracted partner, a personal webmail, or an unknown domain
Run message trace for the sender's other outbound mail to the same recipient in the last 90 days
Interview the sender's manager on whether the send had a legitimate business purpose
containment: Recall or purge the message from internal copies with a compliance search and purge action
Ask the external recipient in writing to delete the message and confirm deletion
Add a transport rule blocking further PII sends from the sender to that recipient domain
Switch the triggering DLP rule from notify to block for the sender's department while triage continues
eradication: Revoke any shared-mailbox or delegate access that let the sender reach the exported records
Remove local copies of the source export from the sender's endpoint and OneDrive
Delete the CRM or HR report export job the sender used to generate the attachment
recovery: Restore normal mail flow for the sender once the business-purpose review is closed
Record the data-subject count and data types in the privacy breach register
Hand the case to Privacy for the notification decision with the evidence package attached
lessons: Measure time from DLP alert to recall and set a target for the next review
Decide whether to require secure-mail encryption for any message matching PII rules
Tune false positives from the rule so analysts trust high-confidence PII hits

splunk.title: Outbound email with PII DLP matches by sender
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype="o365:management:activity" Workload=Exchange Operation=DLPRuleMatch | spath ExchangeMetaData.From output=sender | spath ExchangeMetaData.To{} output=rcpt | search sender="<suspect_user>" | stats count values(rcpt) as recipients values(PolicyDetails{}.PolicyName) as policy by sender

splunk.title: Message trace: sender's external mail to recipient domain
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count values(All_Email.subject) as subjects values(All_Email.file_name) as files from datamodel=Email where All_Email.src_user="<suspect_user>" All_Email.recipient="*@<recipient_domain>" by All_Email.recipient _time span=1d

splunk.title: Other users sending PII to the same external domain
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype="o365:management:activity" Operation=DLPRuleMatch | spath ExchangeMetaData.To{} output=rcpt | search rcpt="*@<recipient_domain>" | stats dc(UserId) as senders count by rcpt

playbooks.name: Bulk upload of company files to personal cloud storage
playbooks.summary: Use when proxy, CASB or endpoint telemetry shows a user uploading a large volume of work files to a personal Dropbox, Google Drive, OneDrive or similar account.

preparation: Enable CASB or proxy instance awareness to tell corporate from personal tenants of the same cloud service
Log upload byte counts per destination on the secure web gateway
Define an upload-volume baseline per user so anomalies can be scored
identification: Identify the personal account or tenant ID used, from CASB instance data or proxy request headers
Total bytes uploaded and file count per destination for the user over the last 30 days
Map uploaded file names against SharePoint and file-share access logs to find the source repositories
Check HR systems for resignation, PIP or recent disciplinary action on the user
Determine whether the device is managed and whether the sync client or browser did the upload
containment: Block uploads to the personal instance via CASB inline policy for the user
Suspend the user's VPN and remote access pending interview if HR concurs
Preserve proxy, CASB and endpoint logs for the upload window under legal hold
eradication: Request through Legal that the user delete the files and sign a certification of deletion
Remove personal cloud sync clients from the managed endpoint
Revoke OAuth grants the personal cloud app holds against the corporate tenant
recovery: Restore the user's access in a reduced role if employment continues
Re-classify any uploaded documents found unlabelled so DLP covers them next time
Confirm the CASB block policy is not breaking sanctioned corporate tenant use
lessons: Add a detection for personal-instance uploads above the user's 95th percentile volume
Review whether personal cloud storage should be blocked by default on managed devices
Track how many days the uploads ran before detection

splunk.title: Upload volume to cloud storage categories by user
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false sum(Web.bytes_out) as bytes_out count from datamodel=Web where Web.http_method IN ("POST","PUT") Web.category IN ("online-storage*","file-sharing*") Web.user="<suspect_user>" by Web.dest Web.user _time span=1h | eval MB=round(bytes_out/1024/1024,1) | sort - MB

splunk.title: SharePoint and OneDrive downloads before the uploads
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype="o365:management:activity" Operation IN ("FileDownloaded","FileSyncDownloadedFull") UserId="<suspect_user>" | stats count dc(ObjectId) as files values(SiteUrl) as sites by UserId

splunk.title: Users exceeding normal cloud upload volume
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false sum(Web.bytes_out) as bytes from datamodel=Web where Web.category="online-storage*" by Web.user _time span=1d | eventstats avg(bytes) as avg stdev(bytes) as sd by Web.user | where bytes > avg + 3*sd AND bytes > 500000000

playbooks.name: Mass copy of files to a USB removable drive
playbooks.summary: Use when endpoint DLP or EDR records a user writing a large number of files to a USB mass storage device, especially from sensitive shares or shortly before departure.

preparation: Enable removable-storage audit events (Event ID 4663 on removable volumes, 6416 device install) via GPO
Configure endpoint DLP to log file names and hashes written to removable media
Maintain an allowlist of approved encrypted USB device serials
identification: Pull the USB device vendor, product and serial from EDR or Event ID 6416 on the host
List files written to the removable volume with paths, sizes and timestamps
Trace the source directories of the copied files to classify the data exposed
Check whether the device serial is on the approved encrypted-USB allowlist
Correlate the copy window with badge records to place the user at the device
containment: Push a device-control policy blocking write access to removable storage on the host
Request physical recovery of the USB device through HR and Security with chain-of-custody form
Isolate the endpoint from the network if the copy is ongoing and the user is unreachable
eradication: Forensically image the recovered USB device before wiping it
Confirm no further copies exist on other personal media through the user interview
Remove any portable archive or copy tools found staged on the endpoint
recovery: Re-enable removable storage only for approved encrypted devices on the user's host
Return the wiped device or destroy it per the media-sanitization standard
Update the data-loss case with the final list of files and classification
lessons: Decide whether read-only USB should be the default for all non-engineering roles
Add an alert for more than 500 files written to removable media in one hour
Review how many hosts still lack removable-storage auditing

splunk.title: Files written to removable volumes by host
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4663 host="<host>" Object_Type=File Accesses="*WriteData*" | rex field=Object_Name "^(?<drive>[A-Z]:)" | search drive!="C:" | stats count dc(Object_Name) as files values(drive) as drives by Account_Name host

splunk.title: USB mass storage devices connected
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=6416 Class=DiskDrive | stats earliest(_time) as first latest(_time) as last values(Device_Description) as device by host Device_ID | convert ctime(first) ctime(last)

splunk.title: Hosts with large removable-media writes
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4663 Accesses="*WriteData*" Object_Name!="C:*" | bin _time span=1h | stats dc(Object_Name) as files by host Account_Name _time | where files > 500

playbooks.name: Source code pushed to a personal GitHub repository
playbooks.summary: Use when a developer pushes proprietary source code to a personal GitHub or GitLab account, or a public scan finds company code in a repo the organization does not own.

preparation: Run a secrets and code-fingerprint scanner against public GitHub for unique internal strings and package names
Enforce SSO and enterprise-managed users on the corporate GitHub organization
Log git push destinations at the proxy so pushes to non-corporate remotes are visible
identification: Identify the external repository URL, owner account, visibility and first commit date
Diff the external repo against internal repositories to determine which codebases were copied
Scan the external repo history for secrets, API keys and customer data in fixtures
Check proxy logs for git push traffic from the developer's host to github.com outside the corporate org
Confirm whether the external account owner is the employee, a former employee or unknown
containment: File a DMCA takedown with the hosting provider through Legal if the repo is public
Ask the employee to delete or transfer the repository and confirm in writing
Rotate every credential found in the exposed code history
eradication: Remove the personal git remote from the developer's local clones
Revoke personal access tokens or SSH keys the employee used against corporate repos if misused
Purge cached forks and mirrors found through code search
recovery: Confirm the external repo and forks return 404 after takedown
Re-run the secret scanner on internal repos to verify rotated keys are no longer referenced
Brief engineering leadership on any trade secrets exposed for competitive risk review
lessons: Add a push-protection rule or proxy block for git pushes to non-corporate GitHub accounts
Remind developers of the acceptable-use policy for personal repos and side projects
Measure how long the code was public before discovery

splunk.title: Git push traffic from developer host to GitHub
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false sum(Web.bytes_out) as bytes_out count from datamodel=Web where Web.dest IN ("github.com","gitlab.com","bitbucket.org") Web.url="*git-receive-pack*" Web.src="<host>" by Web.user Web.url _time span=1h

splunk.title: Corporate GitHub audit: clones and archive downloads by user
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype="github:enterprise:audit" actor="<suspect_user>" action IN ("git.clone","repo.download_zip","git.fetch") | stats count values(repo) as repos by actor action

splunk.title: Push to non-corporate remotes across developers
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype="pan:threat" OR sourcetype="pan:traffic" app="git-base" dest_zone=untrust | stats sum(bytes_out) as bytes by src_user dest_ip | where bytes > 10000000

playbooks.name: Unexpected full database dump or export detected
playbooks.summary: Use when database audit logs or EDR show a full export (mysqldump, pg_dump, bcp, Data Pump, large SELECT *) from a production database by an unexpected account or host.

preparation: Enable database audit logging for bulk SELECT, export utilities and privilege changes on production
Maintain an inventory of service accounts that legitimately run backups and ETL exports
Alert on dump utilities (mysqldump, pg_dump, bcp, expdp) executed outside backup hosts
identification: Identify the database, schemas and tables exported, and the row counts returned
Determine the account, client host and tool used for the export from DB audit and EDR
Locate the dump file on disk and record its path, size and hash
Check network flows from the client host for transfer of the dump file off the network
Verify with the DBA team whether a change ticket covers the export
containment: Disable the database login used for the export and kill its active sessions
Isolate the client host that ran the dump via EDR
Block egress from the host at the firewall if transfer of the dump is suspected
eradication: Securely delete the staged dump files after forensic copies are preserved
Rotate database credentials stored on the client host and in its config files
Remove excessive SELECT grants that allowed a non-ETL account to read the full schema
recovery: Reissue a least-privilege database login for the legitimate owner
Verify backup and ETL jobs still run with the restricted grants
Provide Privacy the table list and record counts for breach assessment
lessons: Add row-count thresholds to database activity monitoring for interactive sessions
Restrict dump utilities to designated backup hosts by application control
Review whether sensitive columns should be encrypted or tokenized at rest

splunk.title: Dump utility executions outside backup hosts
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count values(Processes.process) as cmd from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("mysqldump*","pg_dump*","bcp.exe","expdp*","mongodump*") NOT Processes.dest IN ("<backup_host>") by Processes.dest Processes.user _time span=1h

splunk.title: Large result sets in database audit log
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype="mssql:audit" OR sourcetype="mysql:audit" (statement="SELECT *" OR action_id=SL) | stats sum(affected_rows) as rows dc(object_name) as tables by server_principal_name client_ip database_name | where rows > 100000

splunk.title: Outbound transfer from the dump host after export
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false sum(All_Traffic.bytes_out) as bytes_out from datamodel=Network_Traffic where All_Traffic.src="<host>" by All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_port _time span=15m | where bytes_out > 50000000

playbooks.name: Exfiltration with rclone or MEGA client
playbooks.summary: Use when rclone, MEGAsync, megacmd or a similar sync tool runs on a server or workstation and pushes data to MEGA or another cloud remote, a common pre-ransomware exfil pattern.

preparation: Create EDR detections for rclone.exe, renamed rclone binaries and rclone command-line flags like --config and copy
Block mega.nz, mega.io and userstorage.mega.co.nz at the proxy for server subnets
Ensure firewall logs capture bytes out per session from file servers
identification: Locate the rclone.conf file and record the configured remote type, endpoint and account
Extract the full rclone command line to see which share paths were copied
Hunt for renamed rclone binaries by hash and by the rclone-specific user-agent in proxy logs
Total bytes sent to MEGA or the remote endpoint and the time window of transfer
Look for preceding lateral movement and credential dumping on the host, which signals a ransomware operator
containment: Isolate the host running rclone via EDR immediately
Block the remote endpoint IPs and domains at the perimeter firewall
Disable the account that launched rclone and reset its password
Escalate to the ransomware playbook and check for encryption staging on file servers
eradication: Delete rclone binaries and config files from every host found in the hunt
Remove scheduled tasks or services that launch the sync tool
Rotate credentials for service accounts with access to the copied shares
recovery: Return isolated hosts to the network only after a clean EDR scan and rebuild if tampering is found
Build the list of exfiltrated directories for legal and extortion response planning
Engage counsel on whether to request the cloud provider to suspend the attacker account
lessons: Add application control blocking unsigned sync tools on servers
Alert on any server sending more than 1 GB to a cloud storage category in an hour
Review how the operator gained the access used to run rclone

splunk.title: rclone and MEGA client process execution
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count values(Processes.process) as cmd from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("rclone.exe","MEGAsync.exe","mega-cmd*") OR Processes.process IN ("*--config*rclone*","* copy *:*","*mega:*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name

splunk.title: Traffic to MEGA infrastructure by source
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false sum(Web.bytes_out) as bytes_out from datamodel=Web where (Web.dest="*mega.nz" OR Web.dest="*mega.co.nz" OR Web.dest="*mega.io" OR Web.http_user_agent="rclone/*") by Web.src Web.user Web.dest _time span=1h | eval GB=round(bytes_out/1073741824,2)

splunk.title: Sysmon file creation of rclone.conf
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype="XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational" EventCode=11 TargetFilename="*rclone.conf" | stats values(TargetFilename) as conf values(Image) as image by host User

playbooks.name: Data staged in archives and sent out over FTP
playbooks.summary: Use when a host creates large 7-Zip, RAR or ZIP archives of business data and then opens FTP or FTPS sessions to an external server.

preparation: Deny outbound FTP (TCP 20/21) by default at the firewall except to approved partner hosts
Log archiver command lines (7z, rar, makecab, tar) via Sysmon or EDR
Keep a register of approved FTP partners with destination IPs
identification: Collect archiver command lines to find source paths, archive names and any password switch
Find the staging directory and record archive sizes and creation times
Identify the FTP destination IP, login username and transferred file names from firewall or IDS logs
Check the destination against the approved FTP partner register and threat intel
Determine whether the archives were split into volumes to stay under size alerts
containment: Block the FTP destination IP at the perimeter and on host firewalls
Isolate the staging host via EDR
Disable the account that created the archives pending review
eradication: Preserve and then remove the staged archives from the host
Remove FTP clients or scripts found on the host such as WinSCP portable or ftp.exe batch files
Hunt for the same archive naming pattern on other hosts
recovery: Reconnect the host after confirming no persistence remains
Inventory the contents of the archives from source paths to scope data exposure
Notify data owners of the directories that were archived
lessons: Add a correlation alert for archive creation followed by external FTP within two hours
Review why outbound FTP was permitted from this subnet
Measure total data volume sent before detection

splunk.title: Archiver executions with source paths
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count values(Processes.process) as cmd from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("7z.exe","7za.exe","rar.exe","winrar.exe","makecab.exe") Processes.dest="<host>" by Processes.user Processes.process_name _time span=10m

splunk.title: Outbound FTP sessions and volume
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype="pan:traffic" app IN ("ftp","ftps") dest_zone=untrust | stats sum(bytes_sent) as bytes_out earliest(_time) as first latest(_time) as last by src_ip src_user dest_ip | eval MB=round(bytes_out/1048576,1) | convert ctime(first) ctime(last)

splunk.title: Archive creation followed by FTP from same host
splunk.spl: index=* (sourcetype="XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational" EventCode=1 Image IN ("*\\7z.exe","*\\rar.exe")) OR (sourcetype="pan:traffic" app=ftp) | eval h=coalesce(host,src_ip) | transaction h maxspan=2h startswith=EventCode=1 endswith=app=ftp | table h duration eventcount

playbooks.name: Sensitive documents printed in bulk
playbooks.summary: Use when print server or managed-print logs show a user printing unusually many pages of classified, customer or HR documents, possibly to remove them physically.

preparation: Enable PrintService Operational log Event ID 307 on print servers with document names
Turn on secure pull printing so jobs release only at the device with a badge
Apply sensitivity labels that endpoint DLP can use to block or audit printing
identification: Pull print jobs for the user with document names, page counts, printer and timestamps
Compare page volume with the user's 90-day printing baseline
Classify the printed documents by opening their source files from the recorded paths
Check badge logs to confirm who released jobs at the printer
Review CCTV for the printer area if policy and Legal allow
containment: Restrict the user's print rights to non-sensitive queues while the review runs
Ask HR to arrange recovery of printed material from the user's desk or bag per policy
Enable DLP block-on-print for the affected labels
eradication: Shred recovered printouts under witnessed secure destruction
Purge retained jobs from the printer's internal storage
Remove the user's access to the source folders if not needed for their role
recovery: Restore standard print access once HR closes the matter
Document recovered versus unrecovered pages for the data-loss record
Confirm printer hard drives are encrypted and wiped on schedule
lessons: Add a weekly report of top printers of labelled documents
Evaluate watermarking printed sensitive documents with user and time
Review whether printing is necessary for the affected role

splunk.title: Print jobs by user with page counts
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype="WinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-PrintService/Operational" EventCode=307 user="<suspect_user>" | rex field=Message "Document \d+, (?<doc>.+?) owned by" | rex field=Message "Pages printed: (?<pages>\d+)" | stats sum(pages) as pages values(doc) as docs by user printer

splunk.title: Users printing far above their baseline
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype="WinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-PrintService/Operational" EventCode=307 | rex field=Message "Pages printed: (?<pages>\d+)" | bin _time span=1d | stats sum(pages) as pages by user _time | eventstats avg(pages) as avg by user | where pages > avg*5 AND pages > 200

playbooks.name: Screenshots or screen recording of sensitive data
playbooks.summary: Use when EDR, DLP or VDI telemetry shows repeated screen capture or recording tools running while a user views confidential systems, or captured images appear in uploads.

preparation: Inventory approved screen capture tools and log execution of unapproved ones via EDR
Enable screen-capture protection or watermarking on VDI sessions to sensitive apps
Configure DLP OCR scanning for images uploaded or emailed externally
identification: List screen capture or recording processes (Snipping Tool, OBS, ShareX, PrintScreen hooks) and their run times
Find image or video files created in the capture window and their storage locations
Correlate capture times with which sensitive application windows were in the foreground
Check whether captured files were uploaded, emailed or synced afterwards
Determine whether a phone camera was used if CCTV or witness reports exist
containment: Block the unapproved recording tool hash via application control
Quarantine the captured image and video files in place
Suspend the user's access to the sensitive application pending review
eradication: Delete captured files from the endpoint, cloud sync folders and recycle bin after preservation
Uninstall the recording software from the endpoint
Revoke the browser extension if a screenshot extension was used
recovery: Restore application access with watermarking enabled for the user
Confirm OCR DLP catches a test screenshot of the same screen
Record what data appeared in the captures for the privacy assessment
lessons: Decide whether VDI screen-capture blocking should apply to all regulated apps
Add detection for screen recorders launched on hosts with access to HR or finance systems
Review user awareness training on recording confidential screens

splunk.title: Screen capture and recording tool execution
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count earliest(_time) as first latest(_time) as last from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("obs64.exe","ShareX.exe","SnippingTool.exe","ScreenClippingHost.exe","Camtasia*.exe","bdcam.exe") Processes.user="<suspect_user>" by Processes.dest Processes.process_name | convert ctime(first) ctime(last)

splunk.title: Image and video files created on host
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype="XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational" EventCode=11 host="<host>" TargetFilename IN ("*.png","*.jpg","*.mp4","*.mkv") | stats count values(TargetFilename) as files by Image

splunk.title: Images sent externally after capture
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Email where All_Email.src_user="<suspect_user>" All_Email.file_name IN ("*.png","*.jpg","*.mp4") by All_Email.recipient All_Email.file_name

playbooks.name: Customer list exported by a departing salesperson
playbooks.summary: Use when a salesperson who has resigned or is joining a competitor exports CRM contacts, pipeline or pricing data. Covers the data side; pair with the insider departure playbook.

preparation: Enable CRM report export and API audit logging, including Salesforce event monitoring for ReportExport
Have HR notify Security the day a resignation to a competitor is received
Restrict CRM bulk export permission to sales operations roles
identification: Pull CRM export, report run and API query events for the user over the 60 days before resignation
Identify which objects were exported: accounts, contacts, opportunities, price books
Check whether exported files were emailed to personal addresses or uploaded to personal cloud
Look for mobile CRM app sync to an unmanaged device
Compare export volume with peers in the same territory
containment: Remove the user's CRM export and report permissions immediately
Revoke CRM mobile app sessions and connected app tokens for the user
Preserve CRM event logs and the user's mailbox under legal hold
eradication: Have Legal send a reminder of confidentiality and non-solicitation obligations with return-of-data request
Obtain written certification that personal copies of exports have been deleted
Revoke third-party CRM integrations the user authorized, such as contact sync apps
recovery: Reassign the user's accounts and opportunities to other reps
Alert account managers to watch for solicitation of the exported customers
Provide Legal a timeline of exports for any trade secret claim
lessons: Automate CRM permission reduction when HR records a resignation
Alert on report exports over 1,000 rows by non-operations users
Review whether the export data was needed for the role

splunk.title: Salesforce report exports and bulk API by user
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype="sfdc:logfile" EVENT_TYPE IN ("ReportExport","BulkApi","API") USER_ID="<suspect_user_id>" | stats count sum(ROWS_PROCESSED) as rows values(REPORT_ID_DERIVED) as reports by EVENT_TYPE

splunk.title: Exported CSV or XLSX mailed to personal domains
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Email where All_Email.src_user="<suspect_user>" All_Email.recipient IN ("*@gmail.com","*@outlook.com","*@yahoo.com","*@icloud.com") All_Email.file_name IN ("*.csv","*.xlsx") by All_Email.recipient All_Email.file_name _time

splunk.title: Peers comparison of CRM export volume
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype="sfdc:logfile" EVENT_TYPE=ReportExport | stats sum(ROWS_PROCESSED) as rows by USER_ID | eventstats median(rows) as med | where rows > med*10

playbooks.name: Credit card numbers (PAN) found in application logs
playbooks.summary: Use when full primary account numbers are discovered in application, web server, debug or SIEM logs, putting those systems into PCI scope and risking exposure.

preparation: Run scheduled PAN discovery scans with Luhn validation across log stores and file shares
Mask or drop PAN patterns at the log shipper before indexing
Document which teams own each application that handles card data
identification: Confirm matches are valid PANs by Luhn check and BIN range rather than test card numbers
Identify the application, log file, code path and release that started writing PANs
Count unique PANs and the date range they appear in the logs
List every downstream copy: SIEM indexes, log archives, backups and developer laptops
Determine who had read access to the affected log stores during the window
containment: Hot-fix or roll back the application release so it stops logging PANs
Restrict access to the affected log indexes to the incident team
Pause log forwarding of the affected source to third-party tools
eradication: Delete or mask PANs in Splunk using delete-capable role and document the search used
Purge PANs from log archives, S3 buckets and backup copies within retention constraints
Remove debug logging flags that captured request bodies
recovery: Re-run PAN discovery to confirm zero valid PANs remain in all copies
Re-enable log forwarding with masking rules active
Brief the PCI QSA or internal assessor on the scope change and remediation
lessons: Add a CI test that fails builds when card fields are passed to the logger
Add a Splunk alert for Luhn-valid 16-digit strings in any non-PCI index
Review whether tokenization can remove raw PAN from the application entirely

splunk.title: Candidate PAN patterns in application indexes
splunk.spl: index=<app_index> earliest=-30d | regex _raw="\b(?:4\d{3}|5[1-5]\d{2}|3[47]\d{2}|6011)[ -]?\d{4}[ -]?\d{4}[ -]?\d{1,4}\b" | stats count earliest(_time) as first latest(_time) as last by sourcetype source host | convert ctime(first) ctime(last)

splunk.title: Who searched the affected index
splunk.spl: index=_audit action=search info=granted search="*<app_index>*" | stats count earliest(_time) as first latest(_time) as last by user | convert ctime(first) ctime(last)

splunk.title: Verify PANs no longer arriving after the fix
splunk.spl: index=<app_index> earliest=-24h | regex _raw="\b(?:4\d{3}|5[1-5]\d{2})\d{12}\b" | timechart span=1h count

playbooks.name: Company data posted on a paste site
playbooks.summary: Use when monitoring or a tip shows internal data, credentials, config files or customer records posted to Pastebin, GitHub Gist, Ghostbin or a similar paste service.

preparation: Subscribe to a paste-site monitoring feed keyed on company domains, IP ranges and unique internal strings
Keep takedown contacts and abuse forms for the main paste services on file
Pre-approve with Legal who may download and handle leaked data
identification: Capture the paste URL, author handle, post time and full content to evidence storage
Classify the content: credentials, source code, customer PII, network configs or internal docs
Trace the content to its internal source system by unique field names or record IDs
Check whether the paste author has posted other company data under the same handle
Determine whether credentials in the paste are valid and recently used
containment: Submit a takedown request to the paste service with the evidence reference
Reset every credential or API key that appears in the paste
Block the source of the data if an active compromise path is identified
eradication: Close the access path that produced the leaked data, such as an exposed endpoint or compromised account
Search for mirrors of the paste on other paste sites and request their removal
Remove the leaked data from the internal location it was copied from if it was overshared
recovery: Confirm the paste and mirrors are removed
Monitor for reuse of the leaked credentials in authentication logs for 30 days
Pass the record count and data types to Privacy for notification analysis
lessons: Add the paste's unique strings to the monitoring keyword list
Measure time from paste publication to detection and takedown
Review why the leaked data was accessible to whoever posted it

splunk.title: Use of leaked credentials after paste publication
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count values(Authentication.src) as src from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.user IN ("<leaked_user1>","<leaked_user2>") by Authentication.user Authentication.action Authentication.app _time span=1h

splunk.title: Internal visits to the paste URL
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count earliest(_time) as first from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*<paste_id>*" by Web.user Web.src Web.http_method | convert ctime(first)

playbooks.name: Stolen company data advertised on a forum or leak site
playbooks.summary: Use when threat intel reports company data offered for sale on a criminal forum or listed on a ransomware leak site, with or without a known intrusion.

preparation: Contract a threat intel provider that monitors leak sites and forums for the company name and brands
Pre-agree an executive decision group for extortion and leak response
Retain outside counsel and a breach coach who can engage with law enforcement
identification: Collect the listing screenshots, claimed data volume, sample files and asking price via the intel provider
Validate sample records against internal systems to confirm the data is genuine and current
Identify which system or third party the sample most likely came from by field layout and record IDs
Check whether the listing reuses data from an older known breach or a vendor breach
Search EDR and firewall logs for exfiltration indicators matching the claimed date range
containment: Launch the intrusion investigation for the identified source system if not already open
Reset credentials for any accounts shown in the samples
Avoid any direct contact with the seller except through counsel and approved negotiators
eradication: Close the confirmed access path such as a vulnerable appliance or compromised vendor account
Hunt for persistence on the source systems identified in the investigation
Rotate secrets and keys the dataset would let an attacker reuse
recovery: Prepare customer, regulator and press statements with counsel ahead of any public dump
Track the listing for status changes such as price drops or full publication
Offer credit monitoring or identity protection where data subjects are affected
lessons: Record how the company learned of the listing and how much earlier internal telemetry could have shown it
Add detections for the exfil method confirmed in the investigation
Review third-party data sharing if the source turned out to be a vendor

splunk.title: Large outbound transfers in the claimed exfil window
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false sum(All_Traffic.bytes_out) as bytes_out from datamodel=Network_Traffic where All_Traffic.direction=outbound earliest=<start> latest=<end> by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest | where bytes_out > 1073741824 | sort - bytes_out

splunk.title: Access to the suspected source system by unusual accounts
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count earliest(_time) as first from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.dest="<source_system>" Authentication.action=success by Authentication.user Authentication.src | convert ctime(first) | sort first

splunk.title: Logins by accounts shown in the leak samples
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype="azure:aad:signin" userPrincipalName IN ("<sample_user1>","<sample_user2>") | stats count values(ipAddress) as ips values(location.countryOrRegion) as countries by userPrincipalName status.errorCode

playbooks.name: Data found exposed in a misconfigured backup
playbooks.summary: Use when a researcher or scan finds company backups exposed to the internet: a public S3 bucket, open NAS share, unauthenticated Elasticsearch snapshot or similar.

preparation: Run continuous external attack-surface scans for open storage buckets, NAS and database ports
Enable access logging on backup buckets and storage accounts
Publish a security.txt contact so researchers can report exposures
identification: Confirm the exposed location, its owner, and when it became publicly reachable from config change history
Inventory the backup contents: databases, VM images, file shares and their data classes
Review storage access logs for downloads by unknown IPs during the exposure window
Establish whether the reporter downloaded data and what they retained
Check search engines like Shodan-style indexes for the exposure being catalogued
containment: Remove public access: block public ACLs, disable anonymous listing or close the firewall rule
Preserve the storage access logs and config history before further changes
Rotate credentials, keys and secrets contained in the backup files
eradication: Correct the infrastructure-as-code or template that set the public setting
Enable account-level public access blocks for all backup storage
Delete stale backup copies that should have been purged by retention
recovery: Verify from an external host that the location is no longer reachable
Confirm backup jobs still write and restore correctly with the new access policy
Provide Privacy with access-log evidence of whether third parties downloaded data
lessons: Add a policy-as-code check rejecting public storage on backup resources
Track exposure duration and whether internal tooling or an outsider found it
Thank and if applicable reward the researcher under the disclosure program

splunk.title: S3 access to the exposed bucket by external principals
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype="aws:s3:accesslogs" bucket_name="<bucket>" operation IN ("REST.GET.OBJECT","REST.GET.BUCKET") | where NOT cidrmatch("10.0.0.0/8", remote_ip) | stats count sum(bytes_sent) as bytes dc(key) as objects by remote_ip requester

splunk.title: When the bucket policy or ACL became public
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype="aws:cloudtrail" eventName IN ("PutBucketAcl","PutBucketPolicy","DeletePublicAccessBlock","PutBucketPublicAccessBlock") requestParameters.bucketName="<bucket>" | table _time userIdentity.arn eventName sourceIPAddress

splunk.title: Remaining public storage resources
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype="aws:config:notification" resourceType="AWS::S3::Bucket" configRuleName="s3-bucket-public-read-prohibited" complianceType=NON_COMPLIANT | stats latest(_time) as last by resourceId awsAccountId

playbooks.name: Sensitive data sent to the wrong recipient by mistake
playbooks.summary: Use when an employee reports, or a recipient tells you, that an email or file containing personal or confidential data was sent to an unintended person, often via autocomplete.

preparation: Give staff a one-click way to report misdirected email to the privacy team
Enable external-recipient warnings and delayed send for mail with attachments
Prepare a template deletion-confirmation letter for unintended recipients
identification: Get the message ID, recipients, attachments and send time from message trace
Determine whether the unintended recipient is internal, a known partner or a member of the public
Catalogue the personal data in the message: number of individuals and data categories
Check whether the recipient opened or forwarded the message if read receipts or partner cooperation allow
containment: Recall the message if the recipient is in the same tenant and it is unread
Contact the unintended recipient by phone and request deletion and non-disclosure
Obtain a signed or emailed confirmation of deletion from the recipient
Expire any shared links included in the message
eradication: Disable the autocomplete entry that caused the misaddress in the sender's mailbox
Confirm the recipient has also emptied deleted-items and any mobile copies
Remove the misdirected attachment from the sender Sent Items if retention policy permits
recovery: Resend the content to the correct recipient using encrypted mail
Log the event in the privacy incident register with risk rating
Route to the notification-decision workflow if the risk to individuals is not low
lessons: Track misdirected-email volume by department to target coaching
Evaluate add-ins that confirm external recipients before sending attachments
Review whether the data should have been sent by email at all

splunk.title: Message trace for the misdirected email
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count values(All_Email.recipient) as recipients values(All_Email.file_name) as files from datamodel=Email where All_Email.src_user="<sender>" All_Email.subject="*<subject_fragment>*" by All_Email.message_id _time

splunk.title: Recall and purge actions taken
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype="o365:management:activity" Operation IN ("MessageRecall","SoftDelete","HardDelete","New-ComplianceSearchAction") | search "<message_id>" OR Parameters{}.Value="*<subject_fragment>*" | table _time UserId Operation ResultStatus

playbooks.name: Sensitive file shared publicly with an anyone-with-the-link URL
playbooks.summary: Use when a confidential document in SharePoint, OneDrive, Google Drive or Box is found shared via an anonymous link, and you need to know who accessed it and close it.

preparation: Set tenant default sharing to specific people and require expiry on anonymous links
Log AnonymousLinkCreated and AnonymousLinkUsed events into the SIEM
Label confidential libraries so DLP blocks anonymous links on them
identification: Identify the file, owner, link creation time and link type from the sharing audit log
List every anonymous link access event with source IP and user agent
Check whether the link was posted somewhere public by searching for the link token externally
Determine the data classification and number of individuals affected by the file contents
containment: Delete the anonymous link and any other external links on the file
Move the file to a restricted library if the owner overshared the parent folder
Block anonymous link creation for the owner's site until the review closes
eradication: Review other files the same owner shared anonymously and revoke unnecessary links
Remove external guest accounts added to the site that do not need access
Apply a sensitivity label that prevents external sharing on the file
recovery: Re-share the file with named external recipients if there is a business need
Confirm the old link returns an access error
Record external access counts for the privacy assessment
lessons: Report monthly on anonymous links to labelled content
Enforce a maximum anonymous link lifetime tenant-wide
Coach the owner's team on secure external collaboration options

splunk.title: Anonymous link creation and use for the file
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype="o365:management:activity" Operation IN ("AnonymousLinkCreated","AnonymousLinkUsed","SharingSet") ObjectId="*<file_name>*" | table _time Operation UserId ClientIP UserAgent ObjectId

splunk.title: Google Drive files visible to anyone with the link
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype="gws:reports:drive" event.name=change_visibility event.parameters.visibility IN ("people_with_link","public_on_the_web") actor.email="<owner>" | stats latest(_time) as changed values(event.parameters.doc_title) as docs by actor.email

splunk.title: Owners with many anonymous links
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype="o365:management:activity" Operation=AnonymousLinkCreated earliest=-30d | stats count dc(ObjectId) as files by UserId | sort - files | head 25

playbooks.name: Data loss through DNS tunnelling: scoping what left
playbooks.summary: Use after DNS tunnelling is detected to estimate how much data was encoded in queries, which host and files were involved, and what must be treated as lost.

preparation: Retain full DNS query logs from resolvers for at least 90 days
Force all endpoints to use internal resolvers and block outbound UDP and TCP 53 elsewhere
Record baseline query length and entropy per domain for comparison
identification: Isolate the tunnelling domain and sum total query name bytes per day to estimate data volume
Decode a sample of subdomain labels to determine encoding (base32, base64, hex) and content type
Identify the process on the source host that generated the queries from Sysmon Event ID 22
Correlate with file reads on the host just before query bursts to name the files exfiltrated
Check TXT and NULL record responses for inbound command or file transfer
containment: Sinkhole the tunnelling domain on internal resolvers
Isolate the source host via EDR
Block direct DNS to external resolvers at the firewall if any bypass was used
eradication: Remove the tunnelling client or implant and its persistence from the host
Hunt for the same domain or encoding pattern across all resolver logs
Rotate credentials cached on the host
recovery: Restore the host from a clean image after evidence collection
Document the estimated bytes exfiltrated and the files mapped to them
Provide the data scope to Privacy and data owners
lessons: Add a detection on average subdomain length above 40 characters per domain
Evaluate a protective DNS service that blocks tunnelling patterns
Measure how long tunnelling ran before detection

splunk.title: Estimated bytes encoded in queries per domain
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype="stream:dns" query="*.<tunnel_domain>" | eval sub=replace(query, "\.<tunnel_domain>$", "") | eval qlen=len(sub) | bin _time span=1d | stats sum(qlen) as encoded_bytes count dc(sub) as uniq by src_ip _time

splunk.title: Process issuing the tunnelling queries
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype="XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational" EventCode=22 QueryName="*.<tunnel_domain>" | stats count values(Image) as image by host User

splunk.title: Domains with long high-entropy subdomains
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Network_Resolution where DNS.message_type=QUERY by DNS.query DNS.src | eval label=mvindex(split('DNS.query',"."),0) | eval l=len(label) | where l>40 | rex field=DNS.query "(?<domain>[^.]+\.[^.]+)$" | stats count dc(DNS.query) as uniq avg(l) as avg_len by domain DNS.src

playbooks.name: Suspected data hidden in images (steganography)
playbooks.summary: Use when images leaving the network are suspiciously large for their dimensions, a stego tool is found on a host, or intel suggests data is being smuggled inside media files.

preparation: Maintain EDR detections for known stego tools such as steghide, OpenStego and outguess
Retain copies of outbound email attachments for at least 30 days for forensic review
Have a forensic workstation with stegdetect, binwalk and exiftool ready
identification: Collect the suspect image files and their sender, destination and timestamps
Compare file size against expected size for the image dimensions and format
Run binwalk and stegdetect to look for appended archives or embedded payloads
Check the sender's host for stego tool execution and recently accessed source files
Look for a pattern of repeated images sent to the same external recipient
containment: Hold further outbound images from the sender to the recipient at the mail gateway
Block the stego tool hash with application control
Preserve the original images with hashes before any analysis modifies them
eradication: Remove stego tools and staged carrier images from the host
Revoke access to the source data the extracted payload came from
Strip metadata and re-encode images at the gateway if the channel was image upload
recovery: Release held legitimate images after review
Document extracted payload content for data-loss scope
Close the case as unfounded if analysis finds no hidden content, recording the reasons
lessons: Add a detection for image attachments whose size-to-pixel ratio is an outlier
Decide whether content disarm and reconstruction should apply to outbound images
Review the time spent and false-positive rate of stego investigations

splunk.title: Stego tool execution on endpoints
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count values(Processes.process) as cmd from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("steghide*","openstego*","outguess*","snow.exe","stegano*") by Processes.dest Processes.user

splunk.title: Large image attachments sent to a recurring external recipient
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count sum(All_Email.file_size) as total from datamodel=Email where All_Email.file_name IN ("*.png","*.jpg","*.bmp") All_Email.src_user="<suspect_user>" by All_Email.recipient | where count > 10

playbooks.name: Confidential data pasted into a public AI chatbot
playbooks.summary: Use when DLP, browser telemetry or a self-report shows an employee pasted source code, customer data or confidential documents into a public generative AI service.

preparation: Publish an AI acceptable-use policy naming approved enterprise AI tools
Deploy browser or endpoint DLP that inspects paste and upload events to AI domains
Keep a list of AI providers' data-retention and deletion request procedures
identification: Retrieve the DLP or browser event showing the AI domain, content snippet and data match
Ask the user which conversation contained the data and whether a personal or enterprise account was used
Classify the pasted content: source code, secrets, customer PII, financials or legal documents
Check whether the AI service account had history or training opt-out enabled
Determine whether other users pasted similar data to the same service
containment: Have the user delete the conversation and history in the AI service
Submit a data deletion request to the AI provider where the account terms allow
Rotate any secrets or API keys included in the paste
eradication: Block the unapproved AI domain at the proxy or apply paste-blocking for labelled content
Remove unapproved AI browser extensions from the user's browser profile
Redirect the user to the approved enterprise AI tool
recovery: Confirm with the user that the conversation no longer appears in history
Record the incident and data types in the privacy register
Escalate to Privacy if customer personal data was included
lessons: Measure AI-domain DLP hits monthly to track adoption of approved tools
Include AI paste risks with real examples in security awareness training
Review whether the approved AI tool meets the business need that drove shadow use

splunk.title: Uploads and posts to generative AI domains
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count sum(Web.bytes_out) as bytes_out from datamodel=Web where Web.http_method=POST Web.dest IN ("chat.openai.com","chatgpt.com","gemini.google.com","claude.ai","copilot.microsoft.com","*.perplexity.ai") by Web.user Web.dest _time span=1h | where bytes_out > 20000

splunk.title: Endpoint DLP paste-to-browser matches
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype="o365:management:activity" Workload=EndpointDlp Operation IN ("DLPRuleMatch") EnforcementMode=* | spath TargetDomain output=domain | search domain IN ("*openai*","*gemini*","*claude*","*copilot*") | stats count values(PolicyMatchInfo.RuleName) as rule by UserId domain

playbooks.name: Protected health information emailed without encryption
playbooks.summary: Use when PHI such as patient records, lab results or claims data is sent by unencrypted email to an external party, triggering a HIPAA breach risk assessment.

preparation: Configure the mail gateway to force TLS or portal encryption for messages matching PHI patterns
Train clinical and billing staff on the encrypt keyword or button for outbound PHI
Name the HIPAA Privacy Officer as the owner of PHI disclosure cases
identification: Confirm whether the message was sent over enforced TLS, opportunistic TLS or in clear text
Identify the recipient and whether they are a covered entity, business associate or individual
Count patients and PHI elements: names, MRNs, diagnoses, insurance IDs
Check if the recipient was the patient themselves requesting their own records
containment: Request deletion from the recipient and obtain written attestation
Turn on forced encryption for the sender's department for PHI matches
Preserve the message and gateway logs as part of the HIPAA incident file
eradication: Remove the PHI extract from the sender's local drive and shared folders after preservation
Correct the workflow that relied on emailing PHI, such as a referral process
Remove the external address from distribution lists if it was added in error
recovery: Hand the four-factor risk assessment inputs to the Privacy Officer
Log the disclosure in the HIPAA accounting of disclosures if required
Confirm the department's next PHI sends are encrypted
lessons: Count unencrypted PHI sends caught per quarter
Move recurring PHI exchanges to a secure portal or Direct messaging
Review whether TLS enforcement lists cover all regular healthcare partners

splunk.title: Outbound messages with PHI matches and TLS status
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype="cisco:esa:textmail" OR sourcetype="MSExchange:*:MessageTracking" dlp_policy="*HIPAA*" | stats count values(tls_status) as tls values(recipient) as rcpt by sender message_id

splunk.title: PHI DLP matches by department sender
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype="o365:management:activity" Operation=DLPRuleMatch PolicyDetails{}.PolicyName="*HIPAA*" | spath ExchangeMetaData.To{} output=rcpt | where NOT like(rcpt, "%@<org_domain>") | stats count by UserId

playbooks.name: Password-protected archive sent to a newly registered domain
playbooks.summary: Use when a password-protected ZIP, 7z or RAR that DLP cannot inspect is emailed or uploaded to a domain registered in the last few weeks or never seen before in your traffic.

preparation: Enrich proxy and mail logs with domain registration age from WHOIS or a threat intel feed
Flag or quarantine encrypted archives at the mail gateway when recipients are first-seen domains
Track first-seen domains per user in a lookup table
identification: Record the archive name, size, hash and whether the gateway marked it as encrypted
Look up the destination domain's registration date, registrar and hosting
Check whether anyone else in the organization has ever communicated with the domain
Locate the archive creation event on the sender's host to find the files it contains
Ask the sender's manager whether the recipient is a legitimate new partner
containment: Quarantine further encrypted archives from the sender pending review
Block the new domain at the mail gateway and proxy
Retrieve the archive password from the user or host artifacts to inspect contents
eradication: Remove staged archives from the sender's host
Disable the account if the sender is unknown or the account appears compromised
Revoke mailbox forwarding rules to the new domain if present
recovery: Unblock the domain if it is confirmed as a legitimate partner and add to the partner list
Catalog the archive's contents for data-loss scoping
Notify data owners if confidential content was sent
lessons: Add a detection for encrypted attachments to domains younger than 30 days
Require sanctioned file-transfer tools for sending encrypted data externally
Review the false-positive rate of first-seen domain alerts

splunk.title: Encrypted archive attachments to external recipients
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Email where All_Email.file_name IN ("*.zip","*.7z","*.rar") All_Email.recipient="*@<new_domain>" by All_Email.src_user All_Email.file_name All_Email.file_hash _time

splunk.title: First-seen recipient domains for the organization
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) as first count from datamodel=Email where All_Email.recipient="*@*" by All_Email.recipient | rex field=All_Email.recipient "@(?<domain>.+)$" | stats min(first) as first sum(count) as msgs by domain | where first > relative_time(now(), "-7d")

splunk.title: Uploads to the new domain via web
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false sum(Web.bytes_out) as bytes_out from datamodel=Web where Web.dest="*<new_domain>" by Web.user Web.src Web.url

playbooks.name: Corporate files synced to an unmanaged device
playbooks.summary: Use when OneDrive, Google Drive or Box sync clients on a personal, non-enrolled computer are downloading corporate libraries outside device management and DLP controls.

preparation: Require compliant or hybrid-joined devices for sync clients through conditional access
Restrict OneDrive sync to domain-joined machines using the tenant GUID allowlist
Log device ID and compliance state on every file sync event
identification: List file sync events where the device ID is not in the MDM or Entra device inventory
Identify the user, device name, OS and the libraries being synced
Count files and total size synced to the unmanaged device
Determine whether the user has an approved BYOD exception
Check whether the account was signed in from an unusual location at the same time
containment: Revoke the user's refresh tokens to stop the unmanaged sync session
Apply a conditional access policy blocking sync from non-compliant devices for the user
Remove the device from the user's registered devices in Entra ID
eradication: Ask the user to unlink the sync client and delete local copies, with written confirmation
Issue a remote selective wipe if the device was enrolled with app protection only
Reset the password if the device or sign-in could be attacker controlled
recovery: Provide the user a managed device or web-only access for remote work
Verify the block policy has not broken sync on managed devices
Record the synced libraries and data classes in the case
lessons: Track how many unmanaged sync sessions occur per month tenant-wide
Close gaps where conditional access excluded sync client app IDs
Review the BYOD exception process for clarity

splunk.title: File sync events from unmanaged devices
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype="o365:management:activity" Operation IN ("FileSyncDownloadedFull","FileSyncDownloadedPartial","FileDownloaded") IsManagedDevice=false | stats count dc(ObjectId) as files values(SiteUrl) as sites by UserId DeviceDisplayName ClientIP

splunk.title: Sign-ins from non-compliant devices for sync app
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype="azure:aad:signin" appDisplayName="*OneDrive*" deviceDetail.isCompliant=false | stats count values(ipAddress) as ips values(deviceDetail.displayName) as devices by userPrincipalName

playbooks.name: Corporate data synced by a mobile app to personal storage
playbooks.summary: Use when a mobile email, contacts or file app on an employee phone copies corporate mail, contacts or files out of the managed container into personal apps or cloud backup.

preparation: Apply mobile app protection policies blocking save-as and copy to unmanaged apps
Block legacy ActiveSync clients that cannot enforce app protection
Disable contact sync from managed Outlook to native contacts where not needed
identification: Identify the mobile app, device model and OS from mailbox device partnership records
Check whether the app is a third-party mail client that stores credentials or mail on vendor servers
Review MDM and app protection logs for blocked or allowed data transfers
Determine whether contacts or calendar data were synced to a personal iCloud or Google account
Confirm whether the device is enrolled and compliant
containment: Block the third-party app's ActiveSync device ID or user agent for the mailbox
Issue a selective wipe of corporate data on the device through MDM
Revoke the app's OAuth consent if it uses Graph or IMAP tokens
eradication: Remove the unapproved app's access tenant-wide if it syncs mail to vendor cloud
Have the user delete synced corporate contacts from the personal account
Reset the mailbox password if credentials were stored by the third-party service
recovery: Re-enroll the device with the approved managed mail app
Verify app protection blocks save-to-personal-storage on a test device
Record data types synced for the privacy log
lessons: Inventory third-party mobile mail clients still connecting to the tenant
Add an alert for new device partnerships using unapproved user agents
Review whether contact sync exposure of customer data warrants a policy change

splunk.title: Mailbox device partnerships by app and user agent
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype="o365:management:activity" Operation IN ("Set-CASMailbox","New-MobileDevice","MailItemsAccessed") ClientInfoString="*ActiveSync*" | stats count values(ClientInfoString) as clients latest(_time) as last by UserId

splunk.title: Sign-ins from mobile clients without app protection
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype="azure:aad:signin" clientAppUsed IN ("Exchange ActiveSync","Mobile Apps and Desktop clients") deviceDetail.operatingSystem IN ("iOS*","Android*") NOT appDisplayName="Microsoft Outlook" | stats count values(appDisplayName) as apps by userPrincipalName

playbooks.name: Unexplained spike in cloud egress charges
playbooks.summary: Use when cloud billing or cost anomaly alerts show a sudden rise in data transfer out charges that no team can explain, which can indicate bulk data exfiltration or abused resources.

preparation: Enable cost anomaly detection on data transfer line items per account and service
Enable VPC flow logs and S3 server access logs on data stores
Tag resources with an owner so cost anomalies can be routed
identification: Break down the egress charge by account, region, service and resource ID in Cost Explorer
Map the top resources to owners using tags and ask whether a migration or release explains it
Pull VPC flow logs for the top resources to find destination IPs and byte counts
Check S3 access logs and CloudTrail for large GetObject or snapshot sharing activity
Check for cross-account snapshot or AMI shares to unknown accounts
containment: Restrict security groups or bucket policies on the top egress resource to known destinations
Revoke cross-account snapshot or AMI permissions to unknown accounts
Disable access keys tied to the transfer activity
eradication: Terminate unauthorized instances or functions generating the traffic
Remove unknown IAM principals or roles created during the period
Close public endpoints that should not exist on the resource
recovery: Confirm egress returns to baseline in the next billing hour
Open a billing case with the provider if charges result from confirmed abuse
Document data stores that were the source of egress for the privacy review
lessons: Set per-account budgets with alerts on data transfer spend
Add egress volume thresholds to security alerting, not only finance reports
Review why owner tags were missing on resources involved

splunk.title: Top egress talkers from VPC flow logs
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype="aws:cloudwatchlogs:vpcflow" action=ACCEPT | where NOT cidrmatch("10.0.0.0/8", dest_ip) AND NOT cidrmatch("172.16.0.0/12", dest_ip) | stats sum(bytes) as bytes by src_ip dest_ip interface_id | eval GB=round(bytes/1073741824,2) | sort - GB | head 20

splunk.title: Snapshot and AMI sharing changes
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype="aws:cloudtrail" eventName IN ("ModifySnapshotAttribute","ModifyImageAttribute","ModifyDBSnapshotAttribute") | spath requestParameters | table _time userIdentity.arn eventName requestParameters awsRegion

splunk.title: Large S3 GetObject volume by requester
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype="aws:s3:accesslogs" operation="REST.GET.OBJECT" | stats sum(bytes_sent) as bytes dc(key) as objects by bucket_name requester remote_ip | where bytes > 10737418240

playbooks.name: Partner SFTP account used to pull unexpected data
playbooks.summary: Use when a partner's SFTP or managed file transfer account downloads files outside its normal folders, volume or schedule, or connects from new IPs.

preparation: Restrict each partner SFTP account to a chrooted folder and source IP allowlist
Forward MFT and SFTP server logs including file paths and byte counts to the SIEM
Keep partner security contacts and contract data-handling clauses on file
identification: List the account's sessions, source IPs, files downloaded and byte counts for 30 days
Compare the folders accessed against the account's documented integration scope
Check source IPs against the partner's registered ranges
Determine whether a permission or chroot change widened the account's view
Contact the partner security team to confirm whether the activity was theirs
containment: Disable the partner account or rotate its SSH key and password
Tighten the IP allowlist to the partner's confirmed ranges
Move sensitive folders out of the account's reachable path
eradication: Revert any permission change that exposed additional folders
Have the partner investigate their side for compromised credentials or hosts
Remove stale SFTP accounts belonging to ended integrations
recovery: Issue new key-based credentials to the partner after their investigation
Monitor the restored account for out-of-scope paths for two weeks
Document files taken and their data classes for contractual and privacy follow-up
lessons: Add alerts for partner downloads outside their designated directory
Require key-based auth and disable passwords on all partner accounts
Review contract terms for breach notification from partners

splunk.title: Partner SFTP downloads by path and source IP
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype="linux_secure" OR sourcetype="mft:audit" user="<partner_account>" (action=download OR "open" "flags READ") | rex "open \"(?<path>[^\"]+)\"" | stats count dc(path) as files values(path) as paths by src_ip user

splunk.title: Partner account logins from unregistered IPs
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count earliest(_time) as first from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.user="<partner_account>" Authentication.app=sshd by Authentication.src Authentication.action | lookup partner_ranges.csv ip as Authentication.src OUTPUT partner | where isnull(partner)

splunk.title: Outbound bytes from MFT server per session
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false sum(All_Traffic.bytes_out) as bytes_out from datamodel=Network_Traffic where All_Traffic.src="<mft_server>" All_Traffic.dest_port=22 by All_Traffic.dest _time span=1h
